Volker Turk's term as UN human rights chief extended despite US warnings. [ dawn ]
item.description:
The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday to renew Volker Turk’s mandate as high commissioner for human rights for four years despite strong opposition from the United States, Russia and Israel.

By a vote of 144 in favour, 10 against, and 13 abstentions, the assembly approved the renewal, beginning October 12, 2026, as proposed by UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.

An alternative proposal from Russia to extend the mandate by only a few months, until December 31, 2026, was overwhelmingly rejected, as was the US request to postpone the vote.

Ambassador Jeff Bartos, US representative for UN management and reform, criticised the four-year renewal on both procedural and substantive grounds, accusing Guterres of having rushed the process.

“Make no mistake: If this assembly tolerates procedural overreach, backroom deals, and the misuse of UN posts, there will be consequences.

“The United States will immediately reassess our engagement, participation, and funding,” he warned just before the vote, accusing Guterres of having rushed the timetable “to hand his long-term friend a four-year executive payout”.

French Ambassador Jerome Bonnafont, however, described Turk as “a voice of conscience” who had demonstrated “rigour and impartiality” during his first term.

Turk, an Austrian jurist, has served as high commissioner since October 2022. He has emphasised the universality of human rights and the need to apply international law equally.

During his tenure, he has been outspoken on the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the war in Gaza, Afghanistan, Sudan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Nicaragua.

But he’s also been criticised for not taking more decisive positions on Cuba, the plight of Uyghurs in Xinjiang, China, and for not directly using the word “genocide” in reference to Gaza, unlike several UN experts and rapporteurs.

Turk’s stances have earned him sharp criticism from several governments, notably Russia and Israel.

Both nations’ ambassadors voiced opposition Friday to his renewal, saying Guterres, whose term as secretary-general expires at the end of the year, should have left the selection of the human rights commissioner to his successor.

Does the government have a concrete plan for child safety?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Last month, in my opinion article, “ Child Safety: Beyond Ideological Polarization ,” published in the Dhaka Tribune, I argued that the sexual abuse of children -- including cases occurring within madrasa settings -- is fundamentally a structural governance challenge rooted in weak accountability mechanisms, regulatory failures, and institutional neglect.
The urgency of this argument has become even more evident in recent days. Disturbing content has been circulating on TikTok, featuring madrasa teachers openly sexualizing and objectifying their child students.
Accompanied by provocative comments, this trend reveals a deeper social crisis: The normalization of predatory attitudes toward children and the total absence of effective preventive safeguards.
It forces us to confront an uncomfortable question: Why do these educational institutions continue to fail to ensure child safety, and why does the state allow it?
To answer these questions, we must look beyond surface-level moral failings and examine the institutional architecture within which these abuses occur.
Bangladesh’s response to child protection crises remains trapped in a reactive cycle. After every tragedy, public anger intensifies, demands for justice peak, and political leaders offer swift sympathy.
Following the heartbreaking Ramisa case, the prime minister’s visit to the victim's family and commitment to justice provided necessary, immediate reassurance. Such gestures matter, but they cannot substitute for the institutional systems required to prevent abuse before it occurs.
Before the election, the prime minister repeatedly assured the public, " I have a plan ” for the nation. We must now ask for the procedural details of the plan regarding the protection of children.
We can no longer afford institutional silence, nor can we accept abstract promises.
The current crisis demands a coordinated national response. The government should initiate immediate cross-sector collaboration to develop a concrete, actionable child protection roadmap.
This roadmap cannot remain a policy document alone; it must address the deep, internal layers of madrasa management -- including labour standards, teacher residency rules, child protection training, independent monitoring, complaint mechanisms, and external oversight.
Most importantly, the roadmap must answer practical questions: How will children be protected tomorrow? How will the educational institutions be monitored? What mechanisms will ensure absolute accountability?
A plan on paper is not a plan in practice. The true measure of leadership is not how effectively it responds to public outrage after harm occurs, but whether it builds institutions capable of preventing abuse in the first place.
Our children deserve more than sympathy after they suffer; they deserve a system designed to protect them before tragedy strikes.
Aisha Siddika is a PhD Candidate at McMaster University, Canada. She can be reached at: asiddika@alumni.uwo.ca.

item.title: Citizens should not be forced to do the government’s work. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We must marvel at and admire the residents of the Sreepur upazila in Gazipur. Faced with two decades of waterlogging, blocked drains, and official indifference, they came together, pooled their own money, and built a functional drainage system themselves.
This is a testament to community spirit, resilience, and the determination of ordinary citizens who have stood up and refused to live indefinitely with a problem that should have been solved long ago.
With that said, let us be clear: This is not how a functioning system is supposed to work.
Citizens should not have to become engineers, fundraisers, and municipal workers just to secure basic urban services. The fact that residents had to take matters into their own hands is not a sign of empowerment but rather a sign of institutional failure.
That this has been going on for decades where Sreepur has lived with stagnant water, damaged roads, mosquito infestations, and the daily indignity of a problem that no authority seemed willing to fix is simply unacceptable.
Their initiative deserves praise, but it also demands introspection. When citizens are forced to build their own infrastructure, it shows just how lacking the governance, accountability, and service delivery truly is.
Bangladesh’s urban future cannot depend on communities solving structural problems on their own. Drainage, waste management, roads, water supply -- these are some of the core responsibilities of municipal authorities. When these systems break down, the consequences ripple across public health, mobility, and quality of life.
The Sreepur residents have shown what collective action can achieve. It is time now for the authorities to show that they have learned from this and not just offer praise from the sidelines for citizens doing their jobs. They must ensure that no community is left to fend for itself for decades. They must respond faster, plan better, and maintain essential infrastructure.
To reiterate, this is unquestionably a positive story. But it should never have been necessary.

item.title: Stopping preventable accidents from claiming more lives. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As the world observes World Drowning Prevention Day today, the theme "Unite to turn the tide" is especially relevant for Bangladesh, where drowning remains one of the leading causes of death among young children.
Every year, thousands of lives are cut short by drowning -- a tragedy that is both devastating and, in most cases, entirely preventable.
The scale of the challenge cannot be ignored: Bangladesh records an estimated 18,000 drowning deaths annually, including around 11,000 children under the age of five.
The World Health Organization's call to reduce drowning deaths by 35% by 2035 through coordinated action should, therefore, serve as a rallying cry for policymakers, communities, and families alike.
This is not merely a public health concern but a national development issue that robs families of their futures and communities of their youngest members.
Many of these deaths occur in rural settings where ponds, canals, and other open water bodies are an unavoidable part of daily life, yet basic water safety measures remain inadequate.
What makes this crisis particularly heartbreaking is that proven interventions already exist. Community-based childcare, swimming and water safety lessons, barriers around hazardous water bodies, and greater public awareness have all demonstrated their effectiveness in reducing drowning deaths.
The challenge lies not in discovering new solutions but in implementing existing ones -- consistently and at scale.
It should be understood that preventing drowning cannot be the responsibility of a single ministry or organization. Schools, local governments, healthcare providers, development partners, civil society, and parents all have critical roles to play.
Bangladesh has shown that it can mobilize national efforts to tackle pressing public health challenges, and child drowning most certainly deserves the same level of urgency.
If we truly wish to turn the tide, we must transform awareness into sustained action, so that no family has to endure the loss of a child to a preventable accident.

item.title: No child should be drowning. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For thousands of families in Bangladesh, an ordinary morning can turn into an unimaginable tragedy. A young child wanders out of sight for only a few minutes and is later found dead in a nearby pond, canal, or ditch. Such incidents are heartbreakingly common, yet they are also largely preventable.
Despite remarkable progress in child survival over the past two decades, drowning remains one of the leading causes of death among young children in Bangladesh.
It is often described as a "silent epidemic" because it rarely attracts sustained public attention, even though it claims thousands of young lives every year.
Beyond the immediate loss of life, these deaths leave lasting emotional scars on families and impose significant social and economic costs on communities and the nation.
The encouraging news is that Bangladesh already knows what works. The challenge is no longer identifying effective interventions -- it is ensuring that successful programs continue beyond the lifespan of individual projects.
Prevention works
One of Bangladesh's most successful child protection initiatives has been the Integrated Community-Based Childcare (ICBC) program. Rather than relying on a single intervention, the program addresses multiple risk factors simultaneously by providing safe childcare, promoting early childhood development, teaching survival swimming, and engaging parents and communities in child safety.
The results have been impressive. Across 16 districts, more than 200,000 children received supervised care through 8,020 community-based childcare centres, while around 360,000 children completed survival swimming training. Program reports indicate that no participating child died from drowning while enrolled in these services.
This experience offers an important lesson for policymakers: Child drowning is not an unavoidable consequence of Bangladesh's geography. With well-designed, community-based interventions, it can be prevented.
Why young children are most at risk
According to the National Health and Injury Survey Bangladesh 2024, more than 51 people drown every day, and over three-quarters of them are children. Studies consistently identify drowning as one of the leading causes of death among children aged one to four years.
The reasons are closely linked to everyday life in rural Bangladesh. Homes are often surrounded by ponds and other open water bodies, while parents are occupied with farming, household work, or earning a living. Most fatal incidents occur during late morning, precisely when caregivers are busiest. In many cases, a child is left unsupervised for only a few minutes before tragedy strikes.
These circumstances make drowning a predictable and therefore preventable risk.
Childcare centres deliver more than safety
Community-based childcare centres are sometimes viewed simply as places where children are supervised. Their impact, however, extends much further.
While protecting children during the hours when they face the greatest risk of drowning, these centres also provide structured opportunities for learning, play, social interaction, and emotional development.
This integrated approach strengthens school readiness while supporting children's cognitive and social growth during the most critical years of life.
The benefits extend beyond children themselves. Families -- particularly mothers -- gain valuable time to work, manage households, or pursue income-generating activities without constantly worrying about their children's safety. In this way, childcare services contribute not only to child protection but also to women's economic participation and household resilience.
Swimming as a life skill
In a country defined by rivers, canals, and floodplains, swimming should be recognized as a basic life skill.
Survival swimming programs equip children with practical knowledge about water safety, self-rescue techniques, and basic swimming ability. These skills significantly reduce drowning risk while helping children develop confidence in environments where contact with water is unavoidable.
Integrating survival swimming into broader child protection strategies is therefore both practical and evidence-based.
Infrastructure and services alone cannot eliminate drowning. Families and communities remain central to prevention.
Community awareness initiatives implemented through the ICBC program have encouraged parents to supervise young children more closely, recognize high-risk situations, and adopt safer childcare practices. As awareness grows, behavioural change follows, and with it comes a measurable reduction in preventable deaths.
Sustainable progress depends on keeping communities actively engaged rather than treating awareness campaigns as one-off activities.
Moving beyond project-based approaches
Perhaps the greatest risk facing Bangladesh's drowning prevention efforts is not a lack of effective solutions, but the discontinuation of programs once project funding ends.
Child drowning prevention should no longer be treated as a temporary development project. It should become a permanent component of Bangladesh's national child protection and early childhood development system.
That requires predictable domestic financing. Rather than depending primarily on development projects, proven interventions should gradually be incorporated into the government's recurrent budget so that essential services continue regardless of external funding cycles.
Development partners will continue to play an important role, but long-term sustainability will ultimately depend on national ownership.
Local government institutions, the private sector, and corporate social responsibility initiatives can also make valuable contributions by supporting community-based services and expanding successful models.
A policy choice that will save lives
Bangladesh has already demonstrated that child drowning can be dramatically reduced through evidence-based interventions, community participation, and sustained public investment. The country does not need to reinvent the solution but needs to scale up and institutionalize what has already been proven to work.
Every child deserves the chance to grow up safely. Preventable drowning should never be accepted as an inevitable part of life in Bangladesh. With the right policy choices and sustained commitment, thousands of young lives can be saved in the years ahead.
Mir Masruruzzaman is a journalist and development communication specialist.

item.title: A tribute to Prof Dr Abul Karim. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Born on Friday, June 1, 1928, in Banshkhali, Chittagong to father Syed Wise Uddin and mother Syeda Rashida Khatun, Prof Dr Abdul Karim was a distinguished person with a professional portfolio highly enriched with the composition of academician, education administrator, and former vice-chancellor of Chittagong University.
He was widely prominent as an international historian, epigraphist, numismatist, and researcher of medieval Bengali literature. His academic brilliance prompted him to move forward to study at Dhaka University, where he obtained a Bachelor's honours degree in history and secured first-class in Master’s degree and later embarked on his teaching career in 1951 as a lecturer in the history department of Dhaka University.
In 1958, the University of Dhaka awarded him a PhD degree for his research-based ground-breaking work on "Social History of the Muslims in Bengal" with the then legendary historian Professor Ahmed Hossain Dani (1920-2009) as supervisor. While studying for a Commonwealth Scholarship at the School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London from 1960 to 1962, another successful feather embedded in his professional career cap with a second doctorate for the research work, "Murshid Quli Khan and His Times," under the supervision of Professor JB Harrison. This achievement was the reflection of his eagerness for research and indeed a high watermark in his career curve.
He had a strong footprint in diversified positions from 1962-92. Professor Karim was a Life Member, General Secretary, and Honorary Fellow of the Asiatic Society. In recognition of his service to history, he bagged two gallantry awards: The "Akbar Silver Medal" honored by The Indian Numismatic Society and the "Ekushey Padak" by the government of Bangladesh in 1995.
At the outset of his research work, the history of Bengali Muslims was intensely engulfed by darkness. With utmost devotion, he envisaged shedding light on this dark history. In the face of paucity of source material of medieval history, he adopted the methodology of obtaining Sultanat periods coin reading and inscriptions.
The comprehensive outcomes of his relentless work and diligent research along with the endeavour of researchers who followed in his footsteps helped bring about a paradigm shift to unveil the history of heritage, society, and civilization of the Muslim period.
The journey of history was not confined only in the frame of a vibrant picture of politics and monarchies, expansion and toppling of kingdoms. He as a pathfinder also brought "human history" to the light in the context of socio-cultural and economic standards of living across the border.
Accountability and sincerity also drove him to play a pivotal role in the formation of Bangladesh Itihas Samiti with a view to sharpening and shaping history and transform it to a modern form in independent sovereign Bangladesh.
The field of the research subject he opted was quite difficult due to the severe scarcity of data. In lieu of secondary sources, he had taken the challenging options of coinage and engraving as first-hand primary sources.
His devotion to his work exhibited how seriously he took research as he developed and diversified his linguistic portfolio (Arabic, Persian, Urdu, Charyapad, Sanskrit, and even French and Dutch) to carry forward the research.
Professor Abdul Karim’s dynamic approach of hypothecating and diagnosing articles for presenting the research result possessed unique attributes. He served as an honorary member of the editorial board and contributed to Asiatic Society in the publication of the three volumes entitled History of Bangladesh 1804-1971 .
Dr Muhammad Abdul Mazid is former secretary to the government of Bangladesh and Chairman, NBR.

item.title: India's 'Cockroach Party' takes aim at Narendra Modi's government after national exam debacle. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
India's 'Cockroach Party' takes aim at Narendra Modi's government after national exam debacle

Submitted by Muheet Ul Islam on Fri, 07/24/2026 - 18:52
Paper Leak sparks student protests as anger mounts against India’s Bharatiya Janata Party
Supporters of India's Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) hold placards and chant slogans during ongoing protests, days after thousands of protesters marched towards parliament demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, India, on 24 July 2026 (Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters)
Off

Sitting on the ground and beating a tambourine, Arya Singh was surrounded by a large crowd, mostly students, at a square in New Delhi.

“The government that is incompetent must be replaced” and “Long live the revolution”, the voices chanted in unison, led by the 18-year-old Singh.

For nearly a month, students from across the country have been gathering at Jantar Mantar, an 18th-century astronomical observatory and designated street site for protests.

Protesters are demanding the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, a senior leader of the Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP, and the education minister in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s cabinet. 

The demand comes after the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET), one of the world’s largest medical entrance exams, was leaked; it determines admissions into five-year undergraduate medical courses in India.

More than 2.3 million students appeared for the Optical Mark Recognition, or OMR-based exam contesting a total of 137,000 seats on 3 May.

However, an intelligence report about the paper leak through the social media application Telegram in Rajasthan forced authorities to cancel the exam, and a re-examination was held on 21 June.

Between the cancellation and the re-take, at least 12 students were reported to have taken their lives, according to an investigation by Indian Express, which reported that stress, grief and uncertainty led the students to do so. Further self-inflicted deaths have since been reported.

“Those twenty students who committed suicide had given up all outdoor activities, sports, picnics, everything, to prepare for their exams. This is not suicide, it is murder,” Singh told Middle East Eye. 

“If this had happened elsewhere, the minister would have taken responsibility and stepped down. But in India, he continues to hold on to his position without any accountability,” she added.

The ‘Cockroach Party’

The protests have been spearheaded by what is now known as the "Cockroach Janta Party", or CJP. It started as an online movement and satirical gesture after Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, during an open court hearing, said that “parasites” were attacking the system and compared unemployed youth and activists to pests.

“There are youngsters like cockroaches who don’t get any employment or have any place in the profession. Some of them become media, some become social media, RTI activists and other activists, and they start attacking everyone,” Kant said. 

'They call us cockroaches, and maybe we are, because the system is decayed. What else can they expect such a rotten system to produce?'

- Arya Singh, protester

He later backtracked, saying that his remarks referred to individuals with fraudulent degrees and not to India’s youth, whom he called “the pillars of a developed India”.

His comments drew widespread anger, especially among Gen Z, who are dealing with unemployment, rising prices and growing religious divisions and communal violence after 12 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s rule. 

The movement gained further traction after Sonam Wangchuk, a well-known engineer, education reformer and climate activist from Ladakh, joined the protests in support of the CJP by going on a 26-day hunger strike that ended on 24 July.

During the last days of his strike, the 50-year-old was forcibly removed from the protest site by Delhi Police and admitted to a hospital. 

Wangchuk ended his strike after being assured that the police would no longer use force against protesters, that protesters would not face punishment, and that negotiations with the government would continue.

Singh wears the "cockroach" title as a badge of honour.

“They call us cockroaches, and maybe we are, because the system is decayed. What else can they expect such a rotten system to produce?” Singh, the protester, said. 

“The more rotten the system becomes, the more cockroaches it will produce,” she added, saying that this is why they are “out to show what happens when there is no accountability in the government.”

'Brute force'

Abhigyan, 26, a New Delhi resident who goes by one name, has been among the leading faces of the protest. He told MEE that the movement is against corruption, injustice and intolerance, and accused the government of arrogance.

'This is not the response expected from a democratic nation but from a fascist regime' 

- Abhigyan, protester

He said the BJP-led government has used “brute force” against students through lower-level party workers while senior leadership has publicly pushed narratives painting protesters as “anti-national” or as “terrorists”.

“This is not the response expected from a democratic nation but from a fascist regime, and that is what we are witnessing,” Abhigyan said.

Delhi Police, Abhigyan alleges, used sticks with iron nails to beat students, installed iron barricades with an electric current to give shocks, and used pellet guns to disperse the protest when they tried to march towards the Indian parliament on 20 July. 

The Delhi Police, however, in its post on X, termed such reports as “completely false and misleading”.

Abhigyan says there are three confirmed pellet-gun injuries while 65 people were admitted to Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, of which 15 were in critical condition.

“No person in their right mind and with faith in humanity can defend this, unless their employment depends on it or they are simply paid to defend it,” he said, adding that Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah are responsible for escalating the current crisis.

“The protesters did not have the resources to escalate the situation,” he said. 

'What kind of government is this?'

Far away from the main gathering, another group of protesters sat in a circle, reciting a poem: “Paper leak ki sankiya 80 se bhi paar hai, Kaise sarkar hai, Kaise sarkar hai,” which translates to, “Leaked papers have now crossed eighty. What kind of government is this?” 

'BJP is turning the majority of the Indian population, the youth, against them'

- Vijay Ratawal, aspiring doctor and protester

The students were referring to allegations reported in different studies that nearly 70 paper leaks of various exams have taken place in the country during Modi’s tenure.

“The use of force is making us reconsider whether the BJP should remain in power. There were doubts earlier, but now everything has turned black and white: [those] who want to benefit the common people and [those] who only want to hold the most powerful chair in the country,” Vijay Ratawal, a 21-year-old aspiring doctor protesting with the group, told MEE. 

“BJP is turning the majority of the Indian population, the youth, against them,” he said. 

The families of the protesters, Ratawal said, do not trust the system, as they have seen their dreams shatter not only due to exam leaks but also because of the implementation of policies that go against the interests of common citizens.

“The entire BJP cabinet is incompetent; they have set the country on fire on every front,” Ratawal said, citing the farmers’ protests in Gujarat, the violence in Manipur, and the tribal Chita Andolan (funeral pyre protest) in Madhya Pradesh.

“The need of the hour is to ask the BJP regime to step aside and leave the positions they hold to competent people who will serve the country without greed or lust for power,” he said, adding that the silence Modi shows is a lack of commitment to the youth of the country.

Senior citizens like Jankabi Krishnakumar Nirmohi, a 72-year-old farmer from Bhojpur in Bihar, also took part in the protests. He said that his aim was to support the ongoing protests against what he described as the “dictator mindset” of the Modi government.

“In 1974, the Navnirman and JP movements were launched against rampant inflation, food scarcity and government corruption, demanding systemic political change and workers’ rights. The intensity of those protests was much higher than this one, but the cruelty unleashed on students by the BJP government today has no parallel in Indian history,” Nirmohi told MEE. 

“When parliament loses its way, the streets begin to speak, and that is when decisions are made,” he said.

“The shamelessness of Modi can be seen in his post on X, in which he praised the education minister on his birthday while students were protesting against him,” Nirmohi said. 

“He did not even mourn the loss of the 20 students who died by suicide. The greetings and the blessing wishes show clearly where his support lies,” he concluded.

Gen Z battleground

South Asia in recent years has become a battleground for Gen Z-led protests, resulting in governments being toppled in countries like Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh. 

Sanjay Kumar, an Indian political scientist, psephologist and professor at the Centre for the Study of Developing Societies, or CSDS, told MEE that the youth have sent a clear signal of their unhappiness with the BJP government. 

However, he expressed scepticism about the extent to which the movement can sustain itself.

'When Parliament loses its way, the streets begin to speak, and that is when decisions are made'

- Sanjay Kumar, political scientist

“Yes, the protest is a clear indication that there is unhappiness among the youth against the current government, especially with regard to the NEET paper leak,” Kumar said, adding that opposition leaders also visited the protests in solidarity.

Kumar said he cannot confirm whether the protests were being organised by opposition political parties, as reported by sections of the Indian national media.

“My assessment is that it was neither started nor organised by opposition parties,” Kumar said. “However, once the movement began, [the] opposition saw it as an opportunity and tried to take advantage of it by sending a message to the youth that they are the ones looking after their interests.” 

But Kumar does not see a direct parallel between what is happening in New Delhi and the events that took place in Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal.

“It is not useful to make such comparisons, because those are smaller countries, and something happening in the capital here has very different implications for the country,” Kumar said, 

“If you speak to people in rural areas, which make up nearly 70 percent of the population, I do not think this movement will have much resonance. The momentum is issue-specific and limited to a particular section of the population, mainly the youth of the country,” he added.

Noor Ahmad Baba, a political scientist and former professor at the University of Kashmir, believes that the BJP has not asked for the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, the education minister, because the government does not want to show any signs of weakness.

Meanwhile, Dharmendra Pradhan accused the Indian National Congress (INC), the main opposition party, of using students as political tools and disrupting the Monsoon Session of Parliament.

“Even after the government conveyed its readiness for a comprehensive discussion, the Congress chose political spectacle over democratic debate. Their objective was never solutions for students; it was disruption for political headlines,” he said in a post on X. 

“The students of India deserve far better than being treated as tools in a political campaign. They deserve certainty over chaos, solutions over slogans and responsibility over disruption,” Pradhan added. “We owe our students more than outrage. We owe them answers, reforms and accountability. That is exactly what our government remains committed to delivering,” he said.

But Baba says the government has not faced a challenge like this before and “it does not want to show any sign of weakness by asking for Pradhan’s resignation”.

“It will be interesting to see how the BJP handles this situation,” he added, saying that “having no precedent in the past does not necessarily ensure that a new precedent can’t be created.”

item.title: Indian government seeks time on youth protesters' minister resignation demand. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Leaders of India’s youth-led “cockroach” movement said on Friday that the government ​has sought time until Saturday afternoon to respond to their demand for the education minister’s resignation over exam paper leaks, following talks between the two ‌sides.

The talks came hours after activist Sonam Wangchuk ended his 26-day hunger strike, raising hopes that the two sides could reach a breakthrough after tens of thousands of angry youth converged in the capital Delhi this week to demand the minister’s resignation.

The anti-government protests represent the biggest youth challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi since he came to power in 2014. Opposition parties have echoed the movement’s demands and have disrupted ​the monsoon session of parliament that began this week.

Friday’s talks were held between senior federal ministers JP Nadda and Jitendra Singh on one side, and Saurav Das ​and Ashutosh Ranka, spokespersons of the self-named Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) youth movement, on the other.

The CJP leaders said they had conveyed that ⁠nothing would be acceptable to them without Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation, and warned that without this, protests would spread.

“The government has asked for time until tomorrow afternoon to respond ​on this point (the resignation),” Ranka told reporters. “We hope the government will dismiss Dharmendra Pradhan at the earliest, or that he will resign, so that we can bring this matter to ​a conclusion.”

Minister Nadda said the talks were cordial.

“They had three main demands. We have told them we will meet you tomorrow afternoon and discuss the demands,” he said.

Scattered protests across the country

Besides the resignation of Pradhan, CJP wants police cases filed against protesters dropped, and compensation paid to families of more than a dozen students who local media reported took their own lives after the exam paper leak in ​May.

Although the protesters agreed to hold talks, they had also called for nationwide demonstrations on Friday over alleged police brutality against protesters who marched on parliament on Monday.

While thousands ​of protesters continued to gather at the main protest site of Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, there were reports of scattered protests across the country.

Students, youth activists and opposition supporters staged protests in ‌the states ⁠of West Bengal, Telangana, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, holding placards demanding Pradhan’s resignation and boycotting classes in some places, local media reported.

Parliament was disrupted and suspended again on Friday as opposition lawmakers also demanded Pradhan’s resignation, with no business conducted for the entire week.

The protests by CJP began as an online satire and involved only a few hundred young people when they were first launched. But they grew to pull in millions of online followers when a national medical school entrance test was cancelled in May because the question paper was leaked ​earlier, affecting about 2 million students.

Tens of thousands ​of supporters of the movement marched on ⁠parliament in violation of a ban on Monday and clashed with police when they were pushed back with tear gas and beaten with batons.

Metro stations shut, mobile internet blocked again

The movement’s surge in popularity reflects frustrations among young Indians over issues such as job shortages, as ​well as frequent exam leaks, analysts say.

The Delhi Metro Rail Corp. shut down 17 stations in and around central Delhi on Friday, ​the third time this week ⁠it resorted to such a large-scale closure of the system, which is the lifeline of the capital.

The government extended a mobile internet shutdown in the area until midnight on Friday, two industry sources told Reuters.

The government also defended surveillance by police at the protest site, saying in court that there was no right to privacy in a public space when there is a ⁠legitimate state interest.

Youth-led, ​street protests in neighbouring Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal have brought down governments in recent years.

Although national elections ​are due only by April 2029, key states like the most populous, Uttar Pradesh, run by Modi’s party, his home state of Gujarat, and Punjab, vote next year and anti-government sentiment could have an impact, analysts say.

item.title: India, Pakistan among teams handed direct Asian Games men's cricket knockout berths. [ dawn ]
item.description:
India, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka secured direct entry into the men’s cricket knockout stage at the 2026 Asian Games after the draw was announced on Thursday.

The 10-team men’s competition, starting from September 24 in Nagoya, will begin with a preliminary round featuring Afghanistan, Hong Kong, Japan, Malaysia, Nepal and Oman competing for the remaining quarter-final berths.

Afghanistan, Japan and Nepal were drawn in Group A, while Hong Kong, Malaysia and Oman were placed in Group B. The top two teams from each group will advance to the knockout stage to join the four seeded sides.

The women’s tournament, scheduled from September 17-22, features eight teams and will begin at the quarter-final stage. Defending champions India will face hosts Japan, Bangladesh will take on China, Sri Lanka will meet Malaysia, and Pakistan will play Thailand.

All matches in both competitions will be played in the Twenty20 format.

India swept the cricket gold medals at the 2022 Asian Games, held in 2023 in Hangzhou, claiming both the men’s and women’s titles.

item.title: Brian Lara Stadium hosts maiden Test as West Indies face Pakistan. [ dawn ]
item.description:
West Indies and Pakistan meet at Test cricket’s newest venue in Trinidad on Saturday at the start of a two-match series in which the home side will be enjoying rare favoured status against the visitors.

Brian Lara Stadium, located in the south of the island, has previously hosted one-day and T20 internationals along with regional first-class fixtures.

It becomes the nation’s second Test match venue and 13th in the West Indies, drawing it alongside Queen’s Park Oval in the capital, Port of Spain, the venue of the second Test a week later.

Roston Chase enjoyed his first match and series wins as West Indies Test captain just three weeks ago when the Caribbean team demolished Sri Lanka by an innings and 217 runs and then played out a draw in the second and final Test, both matches played in Antigua.

Chase missed the recent ODI series loss to New Zealand with an injury to his right index finger.

“Roston is a fighter. I know he’s not going to want to miss any Test cricket,” West Indies head coach Daren Sammy said.

“I’m pretty sure Dr. Byam (team physio Denis Byam) has a way of keeping guys on the park, so I’m pretty sure Roston will be ready for the first Test.”

It was their first home Test series triumph since a 2-0 sweep of Bangladesh in 2022, a result which also gave them their last consecutive series wins anywhere as the whitewash of the Bangladeshis was preceded by a notable 1-0 home triumph over England in a three-Test contest.

West Indies are not expected to make significant alterations to the winning combination from the Sri Lankan series, although left-arm spinner Jomel Warrican is likely to come into consideration at the expense of fast-medium bowler Anderson Phillip given the expectation of a pitch favouring spin later in the match.

In-form Ali

In stark contrast, Pakistan have once again revamped their squad in the aftermath of a 2-0 series loss in Bangladesh two months ago with batsman Babar Azam returning as captain in place of Shan Masood in hope of reviving their Test fortunes.

Babar and opening batsman Azan Awais both compiled hundreds in the lone warm-up match against a West Indies Select XI at the weekend while most of the other main batsmen also got confidence-boosting runs.

However the most encouraging aspect of the match in batting-friendly conditions for the tourists was the bowling of pacer Mohammad Ali, who took five wickets in the first innings and will be relied upon, together with the other members of the restructured pace armoury, to give Pakistan a chance to end a miserable run of seven consecutive Test match losses away from home.

Their last visit to the Caribbean in 2021 finished in a 1-1 draw after two Tests in Kingston while the teams’ most recent Test encounters were in the spin-dominant Multan in January of 2025 when the West Indies trumped Pakistan at their own game in the second match to also leave that series at 1-1.

This meeting of two unpredictable sides carries the additional dimension of intervention by the elements as the July/August period is usually one of significant rainfall in the southern Caribbean.

While Trinidad has enjoyed hot, sunny conditions in the days leading up to the first Test, there is certainly no guarantee that such pleasant cricketing weather will be sustained over the fortnight of this short series.
